stem:
An otherwise healthy 5-month-old boy is on day 3 of bronchiolitis. He is taking about half his usual feeds and has had two wet nappies in 12 hours. His respiratory rate is 58/min with moderate subcostal recession, and scattered crackles and wheeze are heard throughout. Oxygen saturation is 92–93% in air, awake and asleep. He is alert, with no apnoeas. The paediatric registrar is admitting him to the ward.

Which initial plan is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: High-flow nasal oxygen for his work of breathing
options.explanation: High flow is for hypoxaemia not corrected by standard oxygen or for worsening respiratory failure. Moderate recession with saturations of 92–93% does not need it, and it does not address his poor feeding.

options.label: B
options.text: Low-flow oxygen to keep his saturations above 94%
options.explanation: Bronchiolitis guidelines recommend oxygen only when saturations stay below 90%. Chasing saturations above 94% prolongs oxygen use and admission without benefit.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Correct. He is taking about half his feeds with fewer wet nappies, so he needs hydration support, and nasogastric feeds or fluids are preferred to IV in bronchiolitis. Saturations of 92–93% are above the 90% threshold, so oxygen is not needed yet.

options.label: D
options.text: Trial of salbutamol, continued if the wheeze improves
options.explanation: Bronchodilators do not help bronchiolitis in infants, and a trial adds treatment and handling without changing the outcome.

options.label: E
options.text: Chest X-ray and antibiotics for the widespread crackles
options.explanation: Widespread crackles and wheeze are typical of bronchiolitis. Chest X-ray and antibiotics are not indicated without features of a bacterial complication.

context: In bronchiolitis, support hydration (nasogastric preferred) when intake falls to about half of normal, and give oxygen only when saturations persistently fall below 90%; salbutamol, routine X-ray and antibiotics do not help.
